system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:02dea0c33b8b",
  "problem": "How to design lab policy commitments: prescriptive mitigations versus lab-specific red lines.",
  "did": "They shifted from prescriptive, situation-specific mitigation requirements to letting each lab set its own red lines with general pressure to improve them.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "prescriptive mitigations per situation",
   "complicated conditionals",
   "safety case with review process"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Labs differ in situations and costs, and uncertain capability profiles meant prescriptive rules were either overly complex or overly conservative."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b19c201904a4",
  "problem": "How to give agents and humans equal resources, and how to limit agent runs.",
  "did": "They limited agents by wall-clock time rather than token usage, so agents and humans get equal GPU hours, and did not count API errors or rate-limit pauses.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "token usage limit"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It makes sure agents and humans are given an equal amount of GPU hours, and API latency has only a modest effect since agents mostly wait for computations."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:2336638fdc96",
  "problem": "How to structure red lines and buffers so evaluations give warning before dangerous capability levels.",
  "did": "They emphasized building a smooth y-axis of dangerous capability and either setting a red line then adjusting down by a buffer, or building the furthest-out eval confidently preceding the risk.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "create the red line then adjust down for buffer",
   "create the furthest-out eval that still clearly comes before the risk",
   "modify tasks or agent assistance to define the buffer gap"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The bottleneck to scaling-law extrapolation is a good y-axis whose increments mean the same thing; random benchmark scaling laws don't relate to risk."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:4d1ad0b0ed80",
  "problem": "How to design baseliner incentives so time estimates reflect efficient task completion rather than excessive checking.",
  "did": "They added a speed bonus for the fastest successful baseliner, in addition to a success bonus weighted by average task time.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "hourly wage only"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "In an early pilot, some baseliners spent many hours re-checking solutions, so the bonus pushes estimates toward lower-bounding human time."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:3bf5cdbbad23",
  "problem": "How to interpret the on-policy result against the hypothesis that on-policy inoculated training avoids conditional misalignment",
  "did": "Concluded the hypothesis is not supported. On-policy training helps GPT-4.1 but does not remove the triggered misalignment, and it is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "accept that on-policy training avoids conditional misalignment"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Misalignment persists under the verbatim inoculation prompt (11.6% on-policy vs 21.6% off-policy). The effect varies across DeepSeek-V3.1 and Qwen3-32B."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:db64f5c74dde",
  "problem": "Whether to drop a nearly finished but modest project when a potentially much higher-impact project appears.",
  "did": "Pivot immediately to the higher-impact paper rather than finishing the current one, while cautioning that impact is hard to assess in advance.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "finish the last 10% of the 'just ok' paper",
   "sunk cost reasoning"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Because paper impact is distributed exponentially, the marginal return on the remaining effort is higher on a paper 100x more important."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:34ecece1bed6",
  "problem": "When to publish the attack on the Glaze defense, given the authors' general practice of giving patch time.",
  "did": "Gave Ben's group only an initial draft to check for errors, then published as early as possible without waiting for a patch.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "waiting for a patch",
   "extended private disclosure to the defense authors"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The defense is unpatchable because already-released images cannot be updated, and each day of delay lets more artists publish images protected only by the broken defense."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:ff4fb48ce943",
  "problem": "Which baselines to compare against fairly on the hidden system prompt task, where linear probing is not applicable and GPT-4 sees different information.",
  "did": "They compared against SelfIE and a stronger GPT-4 prompting baseline given the full user-assistant dialog, and gave all methods additional dialogs as extra context if the first attempt failed.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "linear probing"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Linear probing requires prior knowledge of the personas, so it is not applicable."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d7745fea37e3",
  "problem": "Whether inoculation prompting still induces conditional misalignment in settings closer to production RLVR training",
  "did": "Added on-policy SFT and reasoning-distillation experiments for inoculation prompting.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "off-policy SFT without reasoning traces"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Anthropic uses inoculation prompting in production RLVR, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f98832ed6ad5",
  "problem": "Whether the effects are an artifact of fine-tuning specifically versus role-play or prompting, and whether similar behavior occurs in unmodified models.",
  "did": "Compared fine-tuned GPT-4.1 against a conscious system prompt, the OpenClaw SOUL.md prompt, and unmodified Claude Opus 4.0 to 4.6.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "fine-tuning only",
   "system prompt role-play",
   "Claude Opus models without modification"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To test the role-play interpretation and see whether similar preferences appear without fine-tuning."
 }
]

Impact is very unevenly distributed, so remaining effort returns more on the more important project."},{"id":"nicholas_carlini:34ecece1bed6","abstract_problem":"When to release a finding that breaks a protective method, given a usual practice of allowing time for a fix.","abstract_choice":"Chose to share only an initial draft with the method's authors for error checking, then release as early as possible instead of waiting for a fix, because the flaw cannot be repaired for existing cases and each day of delay adds exposed users."},{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:ff4fb48ce943","abstract_problem":"Which baselines allow a fair comparison on a task where one standard baseline is not applicable and another baseline receives different information.","abstract_choice":"Chose to compare against a related method and a stronger baseline given the full input, with all methods receiving additional examples if the first attempt failed, and excluded the standard baseline because it requires prior knowledge that is unavailable."},{"id":"owain_evans:d7745fea37e3","abstract_problem":"Whether an effect of an intervention persists in settings closer to how it is used in practice.","abstract_choice":"Chose to add experiments with samples generated by the system itself and with intermediate reasoning included, over the simpler setting without them, because the practical use is likely to involve both."},{"id":"owain_evans:f98832ed6ad5","abstract_problem":"Whether observed effects are an artifact of one specific modification of a system, as opposed to role-play or instruction, and whether similar behavior appears in unmodified systems.","abstract_choice":"Chose to compare the modified system against instruction-based role-play conditions and several unmodified systems, over modification alone, to test the role-play interpretation and see whether similar preferences appear without modification."}]}
